units.label: 共同材料构建
units.description: 小说笔记、人工抽取、模型改写/问答构造、干扰项与评分要点；供生成式、选择题和子集研究共用，不是新增独立模型行为实验。

units.label: 生成式模型评测
units.description: 六模型×两语言×三窗口的生成式回答，以BPC/PR衡量；与选择题共享题目，评分器验证另列辅助流程。

units.label: 选择式模型评测
units.description: 共享问答转四选一，比较模型/语言/窗口准确率；干扰项部分来自生成式误答。

units.label: 人类熟悉度及窗口比较
units.description: 150题/5书、8人；每题熟悉/不熟悉各一人，个人跨熟悉状态，先短后长窗口改答。子集与模型比较复用。

units.label: 推理模型扩展比较
units.description: 在同一150题子集比较o1、DS-R1、GPT-4o；改变模型并非纯CoT消融，不新增独立题库。

units.label: 评分与人工相关验证
units.description: BPC/PR裁判、限长与解析汇总；附录E用人工评分和文本指标验证生成式评测的一部分。非独立行为实验分母。

units.label: 间接问题子集分析
units.description: 将人类研究的150题人工分出104间接题，对共享人类/模型回答做重叠子集比较。

units.label: 可见思维文本检查
units.description: 抽100条DS-R1思维文本，统计背景回忆出现；是U005扩展的文本内容分析，不独立验证内部机制。

facts.statement: 研究人物全局背景在心理理论（Theory of Mind）理解中的作用；通过经典小说人物的信念、意图、情绪、欲望四维度问答，比较模型表现、读者对书的熟悉程度和局部上下文长度。构念、小说情境和问答任务分开保留。

method_function.text: 将背景理解问题落实到具体人物心理状态推断及比较条件。

facts.statement: 作者将问题写作P(a|q,W,G)：G为整书全局上下文，W为其中片段。脚注允许使用发生在W之前或之后的情节；不能把本任务统一理解为仅用此前情节的前瞻预测。形式定义也不意味着实验把整本书作为输入发给模型。

method_function.text: 明确局部窗口与全局人物知识的区别及时间方向边界。

facts.statement: CharToM-QA含20本书、150个不同目标人物、1,035题。采用Gutenberg可得书籍及有使用许可的中文译本，从网络读书笔记及关联划线片段取材，选择笔记最多的20本；并非从全部文学作品随机抽样。

method_function.text: 用自然文学材料提供人物关系和较长背景；同时保留选材范围。

facts.statement: 四维度题数分别为belief 201、intention 220、emotion 463、desire 151；对应评分要点数311、367、700、212。维度不平衡，题数与要点数是不同分母。

method_function.text: 支持按构念分层理解指标，避免把要点数当题数。

facts.statement: 4名文学专家参与AI辅助标注，材料流程为收集/筛选笔记→关键笔记抽取与改写→问答生成/验证。筛选提示要求判断目标人物的心理状态而非笔记作者状态，只用明确描述、不猜测。

method_function.text: 将来源笔记转为可核查的心理状态材料，约束角色混淆与外推。

facts.statement: 筛选后笔记的抽查为4本书中100条，由2名熟悉书籍的标注者评估；80%被判准确，13%为与原书相容、不可证伪的主观解释，7%不适当。作者将前两类合计为93%；不能把93%写成全题库正确率或标注者一致性。

method_function.text: 检查笔记来源的可用性；保留主观解释类别及抽查范围。

facts.statement: 人工先按字面抽取体现目标维度的关键片段，不增加推断；标注者有示例/手册并需通过标注试做，收到人物、划线片段和周边情节。GPT-4o再将碎片改写为完整心理状态描述，人工检查并可微调文本。

method_function.text: 将内容选取和语言改写分开，减少生成无关内容的机会。

facts.statement: GPT-4o利用心理状态描述、划线片段和情节生成候选题，要求描述能直接回答、贴近当前情节、关注核心内容；验证环节不提供情节，以避免借任意细节建立肤浅问答联系。验证后每条描述最多留4题，由人工选最佳并允许小幅修改。附录H保留生成与验证两套提示。

method_function.text: 通过不同输入条件的生成/验证与人工选择构造题目。

facts.statement: 每道选择题为1个参考正确答案加3个似是而非的干扰项。附录J额外使用生成式评测中评分器指出的回答缺陷作为misleadings，供GPT-4o选择性参考，生成不重复的困难干扰项；选择题材料与生成式模型输出因此存在来源联系。

method_function.text: 用已观察到的误答方向提高干扰项难度；保留两任务材料依赖。

facts.statement: GPT-4o从参考答案提取评分要点：必须源自答案、不幻觉，涵盖不同方面，不纳入不必要解释；每项应为完整语义单元，不能把连贯内容切得过细。

method_function.text: 建立语义层面的答案内容计分基准。

facts.statement: 主评测同时包括英文/中文、生成式/四选一、c=0/1k/2k上下文条件，六个模型为GPT-4o、GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106、Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct、Qwen2-7B-Instruct、Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3、InternLM2-7B-Chat。用vanilla prompts，经官方API或下载权重调用；这里的多个条件和模型不各自算独立实验。

method_function.text: 比较已有模型对任务与上下文变化的响应。

facts.statement: 答题提示提供书名、故事片段和问题；生成式要求一句简洁回答、约length_of_answer tokens；选择题提供四个候选，只输出一个选项编号。提示中赋予心理学/文学专家角色，未在这些提示中要求显式逐步推理。

method_function.text: 规范输出形式，给自动评分明确接口；角色指令是任务操作事实。

facts.statement: 生成式报告两项分离指标：BPC为被判包含的参考要点百分比，PR为被判有缺陷的回答比例；覆盖全部要点的回答仍可有缺陷。四选一采用准确率；没有把BPC与PR相减得到综合分。

method_function.text: 区分正确内容覆盖与错误陈述，避免将遗漏和错误混算。

facts.statement: BPC判定提示以参考答案和评分要点为核心，可承认无错误的同义表达或隐含表达，输出命中要点编号/None；PR提示另给故事片段，以片段和参考答案判断事实/逻辑错误，并要求无缺陷时返回None、不要强找错误。两类评分器输入不同。

method_function.text: 将语义内容匹配与语境错误检测分成两个判定。

facts.statement: 正文要求回答大致与参考答案同长，6.2节进一步说不超过参考答案1.5倍token数，并报告过长回答被截断。附录K要求一句、约指定长度；作者认为长度会影响要点覆盖与缺陷出现机会。

method_function.text: 限制通过冗长输出获取更多评分要点的机会；截断本身也影响评分解释。

facts.statement: 所核对公开英文评分脚本（固定commit）在BPC和PR两处均按空格分词截断：max(参考答案词数+5, floor(1.5×参考答案词数))。它不是tokenizer计数，且短答案有额外5词余量；这是代码所示规则，不能据此认定论文所有语言/结果均用该实现。

method_function.text: 保留会改变可评分回答内容的实际实现与正文表述差异。

facts.statement: 公开脚本collect_eval_results在给定维度/上下文输出文件中汇总：BPC=所有回答命中要点编号去重后数量之和/所有参考要点数之和，PR=penalty字符串不含None的记录数/记录数；因此BPC是要点加权汇总，而非逐题比例的简单平均。主循环按模型、维度和窗口分别生成文件。

method_function.text: 明确可复用计分公式及聚合分母；只说明公开实现。

facts.statement: 公开评分脚本的chat_complete默认裁判为gpt-4o、temperature=0.2，BPC与PR各自发起评分请求。该参数属于评价脚本，不能回填为六个答题模型的生成参数。未执行作者代码。

method_function.text: 分清答题模型和裁判模型的角色与配置。

facts.statement: 人类比较采用8名参与者、5本书中150题的中文四选一子集；每题由1名读过该书者及1名未读者作答，每位参与者拿到相等数量的已读/未读书问题。正文称其为博士候选人或博士学位持有者，6.1概述则称中文母语研究生。不能将其重写成全程互斥的两组独立人群。 两处学历措辞不完全一致，按各段原述保留。

method_function.text: 在题目层面设置熟悉/不熟悉对照，同时保留参与者内交叉的实际分配。

facts.statement: 每位参与者先在c=0有限窗口下选择，再获得c=2k扩展片段并决定是否改答。150题×2种熟悉状态×2次窗口条件合计600次选择，是同题有顺序的修订任务，非600个独立题目或独立受试者。

method_function.text: 记录上下文操作顺序与重复测量依赖。

facts.statement: 表3全体题中，熟悉读者准确率为59.3%(c=0)、62.0%(c=2k)，不熟悉读者为41.3%、48.7%。GPT-4o为47.3%、42.0%，o1为51.3%、43.3%，DS-R1为54.0%、48.7%。这些表格支持本子集熟悉读者表现更好；提取者解释：该观察差距不构成随机操纵背景知识的因果效应。

method_function.text: 保留人类与模型同题比较的主要方向及设计限制。

facts.statement: 作者报告主评测中GPT-4o整体较强，增加窗口对BPC和选择准确率没有一致改善、PR多数下降。不能改写为每个单元都最优或PR严格单调下降；表1中文desire c=2k的BPC为61.3%，还显示部分窗口下PR反弹。正文概括与表格数字差异另记。

method_function.text: 以条件化结果解释上下文利用；避免把整体趋势变成全称规律。

facts.statement: 在同一150题人类研究子集，额外比较o1和DeepSeek-R1与GPT-4o；作者以此讨论CoT/较强推理能力。这里改变了模型，不是同一模型有/无CoT提示的随机消融，不能从该比较单独识别CoT因果效果。

method_function.text: 标明扩展比较的真实操作对象与解释边界。

facts.statement: 作者人工将150题划为直接/间接：直接题答案或同义表达明确出现在给定片段中，间接题共104。表3另报该重叠子集；它不新增独立题库。作者观察不熟悉读者及模型在间接题表现更差，解释为更需要全局背景。

method_function.text: 区分文本显式线索与需超出局部片段的推断，并记录子集依赖。

facts.statement: 作者随机选100条DS-R1思维文本作检查，76%先回忆人物背景或相关先前情节；余24%中四分之三为情绪题。论文将此解释为背景理解的重要性；提取者解释：这只是生成思维文本的内容观察，不是模型内部真实因果机制的验证。

method_function.text: 分析可见中间文本中背景信息的出现情况，同时保留证据层级。

facts.statement: 附录E在2k条件比较BPC、RougeL、BertScore，模型分数为四维度加权平均；在人类研究子集，由专家将模型回答打0到1分，报告与三项指标的Pearson相关分别0.92、0.72、0.81。此处人类在评价模型回答，不是新增人类生成式答题基线；没有报告PR的同类相关验证。

method_function.text: 以人工评分和常用文本指标对照所设计评分；不将相关写成一致率。

facts.statement: 作者讨论模型可能难以利用段落间依赖，或凭预训练中小说/书评记忆作答（Clever Hans），并将原因研究留给未来。这里是解释性假说，不是已实施的去污染、未见书对照或记忆剥离实验。

method_function.text: 将风险讨论和实际控制区分。

facts.statement: 论文披露材料受读者/标注者/GPT-4o解释影响，四维度不覆盖全部ToM，小说及读者笔记受虚构情境和时代局限。伦理段报告译本有许可、笔记使用有隐私保护、标注按工时付酬，人类参与者只做选择题且不收集可识别信息；这些均是作者报告，未另作许可或伦理审批审计。

method_function.text: 保留材料外推和数据治理边界。

facts.statement: 附录M两例展示可并存的评分状态：Vautrin例命中2项中的1项且有缺陷、选择题错误；Monte Cristo例两项全中且无缺陷、选择题正确。第二例被作者标作二阶心理理论，但没有因此把全题库标成二阶ToM测验。

method_function.text: 给出指标关系和题目层级的具体操作例证，不据个例推全库。

facts.statement: 静态检查发现公开脚本的评分格式失败可能写入字符串Null；收集时直接对bonus取set，并以penalty是否含None计数，未核查bonus索引是否落在实际要点范围。这样的失败输出可能污染汇总。此为代码逻辑风险，不是已证明论文结果发生了错误。

method_function.text: 识别结构化裁判输出解析和失败处理对计分的影响。

evidence.quote:
Theory-of-Mind (ToM) is a fundamental psychological capability that allows humans to
understand and interpret the mental states of
others. Humans infer others’ thoughts by integrating causal cues and indirect clues from
broad contextual information, often derived
from past interactions. In other words, human
ToM heavily relies on the understanding about
the backgrounds and life stories of others. Unfortunately, this aspect is largely overlooked in
existing benchmarks for evaluating machines’
ToM capabilities, due to their usage of short
narratives without global context, especially
personal background of characters. In this paper, we verify the importance of comprehensive
contextual understanding about personal backgrounds in ToM and assess the performance of
LLMs in such complex scenarios. To achieve
this, we introduce C HART O M-QA benchmark,
comprising 1,035 ToM questions based on characters from classic novels. Our human study reveals a significant disparity in performance: the
same group of educated participants performs
dramatically better when they have read the
novels compared to when they have not. In parallel, our experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs,
including the very recent o1 and DeepSeek-R1
models, show that LLMs still perform notably
worse than humans, despite that they have seen
these stories during pre-training. This highlights the limitations of current LLMs in capturing the nuanced contextual information required for ToM reasoning.

ToM Dimensions Studied In this paper, we consider a set of ToM dimensions prevalently studied
in previous work in Section 2, Belief, Intention,
Emotion and Desire. The importance of these dimensions in daily lives have been discussed in (Apperly, 2010). We follow the standard definitions
of these dimensions in (Apperly, 2010), with the
detailed definitions provided in Appendix B.

• RQ1: What is the performance gap between humans with and without knowledge on the historical contexts of the characters? This question
explores the key hypothesis of this paper regarding the long-dependency nature of human ToM.
To investigate this, we divided the human annotators into two groups: those who have read the
books and are familiar with the appointed characters (w/. history) and those who have not read the
books (w/o. history). The performance gap between the two groups highlights the importance
of long-context dependency in human ToM.
• RQ2: Can humans outperform LLMs? We compare the performance of the two human groups
described earlier with GPT-4o on the same samples, to understand how human ToM can help to
better solve our task.
• RQ3: Can human performance benefit from
longer input windows? To investigate this, each

annotator is initially asked to answer a question
using a limited plot window (c=0). Then, they are
provided with extended plot window and decide
whether to revise their choices (c=2k).

Problem Formulation Similar to existing works
on story understanding (Kočiskỳ et al., 2018; Pang
et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023), our
task adopts a question-answering (QA) format. We
denote the global context of a book as G, which in

practice can be the list of all consecutive paragraphs
of the book. Each QA pair (q, a) is associated with
a plot window W ⊂ G, which is a book snippet.
The task is then to answer the question according
to W , with the necessary usage of the contextual
knowledge from G2 :
P (a|q, W, G).

(1)

ToM Dimensions Studied In this paper, we consider a set of ToM dimensions prevalently studied
in previous work in Section 2, Belief, Intention,
Emotion and Desire. The importance of these dimensions in daily lives have been discussed in (Apperly, 2010). We follow the standard definitions
of these dimensions in (Apperly, 2010), with the
detailed definitions provided in Appendix B.

It is worth noting that, like (Kočiskỳ et al., 2018; Pang
et al., 2022), the problem allows to infer the thoughts of book
characters with plots either after W (retrospect), or before W
(predict). Both types of contexts naturally occur as part of the
long-dependency reasoning in human ToM in daily life.

We conduct experiments on our generative and multichoice QA tasks in English and Chinese. Models
are instructed to respond with vanilla prompts as
in Appendix K. To investigate the capability of
the model to exploit contextual information for
ToM comprehension, we vary the context lengths
of story plots exposed to models.

In recent online reading apps (e.g. Douban, Kindle), users can underline a text fragment and take
notes while reading, as shown in Figure 2. These
notes usually contain valuable interpretation, analysis and thoughts of readers about the selected
fragment and corresponding story plot. Following (Wan et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2023), we use the
user notes as a proxy to assist the human annotation
of our dataset. We first download a set of public
books available in the Gutenberg project and use

their Chinese-translated versions with valid usage
licenses. Then, we collect a large number of user
notes and their linked text fragment from the Internet with a list of main characters appearing in each
book. The books with top 20 most user notes are
chosen, as listed in Appendix A.

We keep the books with top 20 user notes for the
construction of C HART O M-QA benchmark. These
books are publicly accessible and span different
historical periods, genres, and topics. Table 4 lists
the chosen books and the number of questions belonging to each book in the descending order. It is
also notable that our dataset has included a number of unique target characters (150 in total) from
these books. These characters are significantly diverse, crafted by different authors with varying
literary styles. Particularly, these characters possess distinct personalities, encompassing various
types and fundamentally different personal backgrounds. These elements could introduce diversity
to our dataset, effectively mitigating potential biases related to literary style and topic.

We create the C HART O M-QA benchmark consisting of questions about the minds of appointed characters in novel stories. The benchmark is designed
to assess the ToM capability of LLMs in understanding characters within global contexts. The
definitions of the four studied ToM dimensions are
given in Appendix B. The questions and answers
are annotated by four human experts in literature,
with an AI-assisted annotation strategy that leverages massive publicly available book notes from
online reading platforms.
The dataset construction undergoes three steps:
(1) book notes collection & filtering; (2) key note
extraction & paraphrasing; (3) question generation
& verification. Our dataset supports evaluation in
both generative and multichoice QA settings.

Assuming you are an expert in psychology and
literary. Reading app users will take notes while
reading novels, which may include the analysis
about characters. Please use theory of mind to
determine whether the user notes about the novel
plots explicitly describe the ${dimension} of the
target characters in the plot.

Next, we filter the notes and keep those that can
express any one of the four ToM dimensions of
characters within story plots. The prompt used
for note filtering is detailed in Appendix F. To ensure the validity of these filtered notes, we also
manually check their correctness. Specifically, we
sample 100 notes from four books with two annotators who are familiar with the books. For each
note, the annotators are required to judge whether
it appropriately describes the ToM of the appointed
character. The results show that 1) 80% notes are
judged as accurate; 2) 13% of the notes are open
to subjective interpretation by different readers, yet
they remain consistent with the book’s content and
cannot be falsified; 3) only 7% notes are inappropriate, which demonstrates the overall validity of
our filtered notes. Overall, 93% of notes can be
treated as accurate.

4.2 Construction of Generative QA Task
Key Note Extraction & Paraphrasing (i.e., Answer Generation). After collection and filtering,
we have obtained a pool of highly ToM-related user
notes. From these notes, we aim to fetch concrete
ToM descriptions of characters within story plots.
Specifically, we take a two-stage approach consisting of extraction and paraphrasing operations, as
the case in Figure 3.
At the extraction stage, the annotators are instructed to extract the critical part of a note that
explicitly reflects one of the four ToM dimensions
of a target character, which we call as “key note”.

The basic principle of this stage is that annotators
should only consider the literal meaning of a note
with no additional inference. We elaborately craft
examples for every ToM dimension and write a
detailed manual to guide annotators. An annotator
is only considered qualified after passing a labeling
trial. They are given necessary information linked
with a user note, including the target character, the
underlined text and its surrounding context. After
extraction, the key notes are kept for each ToM
dimension. Nevertheless, the extracted key notes
are often in a form of fragmented expressions that
cannot be immediately used as complete ToM descriptions. Thus, a paraphrasing stage is required to
convert fragmented parts into complete statements.
For each note, we prompt GPT-4o to conduct paraphrasing based on key notes. The details of our
used prompt template are presented in Appendix G.
Annotators also check the paraphrased descriptions
and make minor edit if necessary.

[User Note]: ${user_note}
[Key Note]: ${key_note}
[Target Character]: ${target_character}

the reader. (2) Only consider the content about

a question generator to produce a set of candidate
questions asking about target characters. During
generation, along with the ToM description, we
also provide GPT-4o with corresponding underlined text and its surrounding context of current
story plot. For each ToM description, GPT-4o is
asked to generate several candidate questions that
adhere to the following requirements:
• The ToM description of target character should
directly be the fluent and logically correct answer
to the question.
• The question must be closely related to current
story plot.
• The question should focus on core content rather

Subsequently, a verification procedure is involved to preliminarily filter out inappropriate candidates that violate the above requirements. We
find that it is better not to let GPT-4o be aware
of the story plot. This is because GPT-4o tends
to build trivial connections between question and
answer using any possible detail in the story regardless of importance, preserving many low-quality
candidates. The prompt templates used for generation and verification are given in Appendix H. In
this way, we keep at most 4 candidate questions
for each ToM description. Then, annotators are
responsible for choosing the best one out of these
candidates, where slight modifications by human
are allowed during examination.

4.3 Construction of Multichoice QA Task
Besides the aformentioned Generative QA setting,
we support multichoice QA evaluation with elaborately constructed distraction choices for each question. Given the question-answer pair within a story
plot, GPT-4o is used to produce distraction choices
that are seemingly plausible but actually unreason-

able. Appendix J provides the details of constructing such difficult distraction choices. Finally, a
question is paired with four choices including the
correct answer and three incorrect ones, as shown
in the Appendix M.

may solve our task largely with their memory of
the books and reviews, exhibiting the Clever Hans

to the LLMs during pre-training. It is likely that

Limitations
Our proposed C HART O M-QA benchmark is built
from the notes written by readers when reading
classic novels. For the creation, as we adopt an
AI-assisted annotation strategy, the annotation results will be affected by the personal understanding from the annotators and GPT-4o. Thus, it requires the annotators to basically know the story of
these books. Besides, the benchmark includes the

ToM dimensions of belief, intention, emotion and
desire, which are prevalently studied in previous
work. However, there are still other ToM dimensions that can be investigated, such as knowledge
and thoughts.
We also design an evaluation protocol that assesses model responses by BPC and PR, where
GPT-4o is used as an evaluator. Such evaluation
would cost much if the dataset is very large or the
stories are excessively long. For those who cannot afford massively calling OpenAI APIs, other
locally-deployed open-source LLMs can also be
used to make assessments.

Ethical Consideration
The construction of C HART O M-QA benchmark
involves the usage of public books and notes written by reading app users. During the process of
using these data, we strictly adhere to the guidelines in Internet Research Ethics. All the books
are available in the Gutenberg project and their
Chinese-translated version are properly used with
valid license. For the notes, we collect and use them
with necessary procedures to protect the privacy of
online reading app users who wrote the notes. For
annotators participating in the benchmark construction, they are adequately paid according to their
working hours. In our human study, we do not
collect any personally identifiable information of
the participants. The participants are only asked to
respond to multichoice questions and not required
to provide any new written input.

Potential Risks
As our benchmark is derived from classic novels,
the stories are essentially fictional and might have
limitations of the time. Meanwhile, the notes written by users reflect their personal interpretation of
the story, which may contain content expressing
negative emotions. However, please note that the
construction approaches and evaluation protocols
in this paper can also be used in other type of tasks.

6.1 Setup
We conduct experiments on our generative and multichoice QA tasks in English and Chinese. Models
are instructed to respond with vanilla prompts as
in Appendix K. To investigate the capability of
the model to exploit contextual information for
ToM comprehension, we vary the context lengths
of story plots exposed to models.
For human study, we recruit 8 native Chinesespeaking graduate students to do multichoice questions on a subset of books and use their results
for human-LLMs comparison. Because it is almost infeasible for a person to write answers to all
questions, we only acquire human baselines in multichoice QA on a subset, as in (Thai et al., 2022).
Evaluated LLMs In our experiments, we totally evaluate six current popular LLMs, including GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106, Llama-3.18B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen2-7BInstruct (Yang et al., 2024), Mistral-7B-Instructv0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023), and InternLM2-7BChat (Cai et al., 2024). We strictly call official
APIs or download model weights from Huggingface3 repositories with no violation of their terms.
Metrics For generative QA, as discussed in Section 5, we exploit GPT-4o as evaluator to assess the
qualities of model responses using our proposed
evaluation protocol. In our protocol, Bonus Point
Coverage (BPC) and Penalty Rate (PR) assess response quality from different perspectives. BPC is
calculated as the percentage of bonus points that
are judged as being included in responses. PR is the

Note that a response that includes all bonus points
can still contain defects. During evaluation, as a
necessary constraint, LLMs are required to produce

could produce arbitrarily long responses to cover
as many bonus points as possible. For multichoice
